title: One Region, More Arrows
takeaway: A hand-drawn schematic of what the paper means by feature splitting: widening the autoencoder does not send new features off to new parts of activation space, it packs more dictionary directions into the same narrow cone, so the split features end up at small angles to one another. It is an illustration of the authors' picture, not a measurement.
walkthrough:
### What you are looking at

Three panels sit side by side. The label running across the top — "Increasing number of learned sparse features" — tells you how they are ordered. Each panel stands for one [[dictionary-learning-run]]: one trained [[sparse-autoencoder]], with its own fixed number of learned features. Moving right means a wider autoencoder, so more directions to spend on the same activations.

Inside each panel there is a grey blob and a fan of arrows. The blob is a schematic patch of activation space — in the real experiments that space holds the transformer's MLP activation vectors, and the drawing flattens it to two dimensions. Each arrow is a [[feature-direction]]: the unit vector along which one feature writes when it fires. All the arrows share a tail, because directions are measured from a common origin.

The arrows come in two shades, and the difference carries the whole argument. The faint grey arrows sit in the same three positions in every panel. They stand for the paper's conjectured [[true-features]] — the idealized set the authors think [[dictionary-learning]] would return if the dictionary could be unlimited in size. The bold black arrows are what this particular run actually learned.

### How to read it

Count the black arrows, panel by panel. The left panel has one, and it sits in the middle of the grey fan rather than on any single grey arrow. The middle panel has two, each now close to one of the outer grey arrows. The right panel has three, each lying essentially on top of a grey one.

### What it shows

The grey blob does not grow, and the fan does not widen. Only the black count changes.

That is the geometric content of [[feature-splitting]]: extra dictionary capacity is spent subdividing territory that was already covered, and the resulting directions sit at small mutual angles. The paper's reading of the coarse panel is that its single direction covers roughly the same ground as the idealized set, at the cost of being less specific.

The concrete case behind the picture is base64: one base64 feature in A/0, three in A/1, many more in A/2. The measured counterpart is the neighbouring UMAP figure, where conceptually similar features do land in tight clusters — this panel is the cartoon of that result, drawn after the fact. The paper also notes the real refinement is not a clean tree, since features at one size can both split and merge to form the next size's features.

terms.term: Increasing number of learned sparse features
terms.definition: The header label spanning all three panels. It states the only variable that changes from left to right: the width of the sparse autoencoder, i.e. how many feature directions the dictionary is allowed to contain.
The label at the top right, with an arrow pointing rightward. It names the phenomenon the panel sequence is meant to depict and reinforces the left-to-right reading order.
One of the three drawings. Each stands for a separate trained autoencoder over the same transformer activations, differing only in how many features it was given.

The blob each fan of arrows points into. It is a schematic patch of activation space — the territory that this cluster of related features covers. It is drawn identically in all three panels to make the point that the territory does not change.
The vector space the decomposition is fit to. In this paper it is the space of the one-layer transformer's MLP activations, which has 512 dimensions; the figure shows it as a 2-D plane.
A dictionary direction that this run actually learned — a column of the autoencoder's decoder matrix, constrained to unit length. Their count is what increases across the panels.

One of the conjectured idealized features the authors imagine dictionary learning would recover with an unlimited dictionary. The same three are drawn in every panel as a fixed backdrop; in the rightmost panel the black arrows cover them.

The single point at the right of each panel from which every arrow emanates. It represents the origin of activation space, since a feature direction is a direction from the origin and its tail position carries no information.

The narrowness of the fan. This is the figure's claim about geometry: split features are not scattered, they sit close together in direction, so the cosine similarity between their dictionary vectors is high.

One hidden unit of the sparse autoencoder, consisting of a scalar activation that is zero on most tokens plus a fixed direction it writes along. This is the unit the paper wants to interpret in place of a neuron.

The full set of directions the autoencoder may use to reconstruct an activation vector. Here it is deliberately larger than the number of neurons, which is what makes the extra arrows in later panels possible.
The paper's name for what the sequence depicts: as the dictionary is widened, a feature found in a coarse run is replaced by several more specific ones covering approximately the same activations.

The paper's names for the runs this schematic abstracts. 'A' is the transformer, and the second number indexes the dictionary learning run; A/0 through A/5 hold the L1 coefficient fixed and increase dictionary size.

The hypothesis motivating the whole picture: the model represents more features than it has neurons by assigning each a direction, accepting that the directions cannot all be orthogonal. Tight clusters of near-parallel directions are what the paper calls very tight superposition.

numbers.meaning: Number of panels. Three is enough to show a trend — one direction, then two, then three — without the figure claiming any particular schedule of dictionary sizes.
Bold black arrows in the left, middle and right panels respectively. These are the directions the run learned; the increase from panel to panel is the entire content of the drawing.

Faint grey arrows, held in the same positions in all three panels. They represent the idealized feature set, which by assumption does not change when you retrain a wider autoencoder — so the rightmost run has finally resolved all of them.
Dictionary size of A/0, the coarsest run the schematic's left panel stands for. It equals the transformer's MLP width, so A/0 is not overcomplete: it has exactly as many features as neurons.
Dictionary size of A/1, the run the paper focuses on most. It is an 8x expansion over the 512 neurons, which the paper calls a modest expansion factor.
Dictionary size of A/2, the finest of the three runs used in the feature-splitting analysis — a 32x expansion.

The count of base64-specific features found in A/0, A/1 and A/2. This is the concrete observation the schematic generalizes: A/0/45 fires on all base64 tokens, and in A/1 it splits into one feature preferring letters, one preferring digits, and one firing on base64 that decodes to ASCII text.

The full range of autoencoder widths the paper trained, expressed as a multiple of the 512-neuron MLP. The schematic implies the trend continues past the three panels drawn; 256x is the largest expansion reported.

The masked cosine similarity threshold used in the adjacent worked example to decide whether a feature in one run is a split-off of a feature in a coarser run. It does not appear in this figure; the authors say they picked it to keep the resulting graph small enough to read while still showing structure, which makes it a presentation choice rather than a measured cutoff.
